## TL;DR

Remote validation now accepts a project-owned check command on both native and Docker runners. During review, a Docker ENTRYPOINT interaction was found that could make the custom gate return green without running the project command. I changed the custom Docker invocation and its tool probe to select Bash explicitly, added an end-to-end runner-script test with a fake Docker CLI, and kept Docker startup/setup errors distinct from genuine project exit codes. The host pool also no longer presents `native` as a job-routing capability, matching the documented contract that `runner` selects implementation while `os` and labels describe capabilities.

The final `repoos check --changed main` passed. It built and ran the scoped suite remotely on ThinkPad, including 566 selected test files, then passed local format, lint, and other applicable guards. The end-to-end Docker test and the host-pool tests also passed locally. No live Tiao Android/Gradle run or live multi-host run was performed in this session.

## Work and rationale

The original feature extended the remote validation path beyond RepoOS's fixed Bun sequence. `remoteValidation.command` is forwarded to the runner, the host probe checks declared tools for the configured runner, and the command's output and artifacts flow through the existing validation result. Native hosts can use a login shell and user-level toolchains; Docker hosts execute inside the configured image with persistent cache mounts. The Settings UI exposes the command and required tools, and the documentation gives a Gradle/Android and web example. The pool queues jobs across eligible hosts and can fall back to the local plan when configured.

The automated review showed why checking only generated command text was insufficient. The `repoos-ci` image defines `ENTRYPOINT ["/bin/bash", "-lc"]`. Supplying `bash -lc <script>` after the image therefore passes an extra command to that entrypoint; Bash can exit successfully without evaluating the intended script. The declared-tool probe had the same issue, so it could falsely report required tools as present. Both Docker invocations now use `--entrypoint bash` and then provide `-lc` with the intended command. This makes the argument sequence explicit and works with images that define an ENTRYPOINT.

To guard the actual runner behavior, I added a test that creates a temporary git repository and bundle, invokes `scripts/remote-runner/validate.sh` with a fake Docker executable, records Docker's received arguments, and simulates the explicit Bash entrypoint. The test verifies both the argv sequence and that a fixture project command writes its expected output to the returned artifacts log. This exercises the Docker branch end to end without Docker, SSH, credentials, or a project-specific runner.

The custom Docker path previously printed `[validate] gate exit N` for every Docker return code. That erased the distinction between a project test failure and an image/container startup failure, and it did not preserve the stock path's reserved setup codes. The path now maps Docker CLI startup codes 125, 126, and 127 to the existing container setup exit code 5. It writes a gate-start marker into the artifact log only after setup has succeeded, emits the gate-exit marker only when that marker exists, and maps an exit 4 before the gate starts to the existing setup failure code. A project command that itself returns 3, 4, or 5 still receives the gate marker and remains a project failure for classification.

The runner's execution mode is a host detail. `hostCapabilities` now exposes only the configured OS and labels; `runner = "native"` no longer becomes a value that a check step could request via `runsOn`. The pool test checks that a native Linux host satisfies `linux` and does not satisfy `native`, consistent with the docs and type contract.

## Approaches tried

I first checked the error against the image definition and the exact Docker argv in the custom branch. The issue came from Docker's configured entrypoint and argument composition, so the fix makes the executable selection explicit instead of relying on image defaults. I updated the probe in the same way to avoid a separate false-green health check.

For regression coverage, I considered checking for `--entrypoint` in the generated shell, but that would repeat the weakness called out in review: textual presence does not prove that the intended command is passed in the correct position or run. The fake-Docker test instead executes the full validation script and evaluates the command received after the `--entrypoint bash IMAGE -lc` sequence.

## Challenges and blockers

The first changed-path check found formatting issues in the new test. I ran `bun run fmt`, confirmed it changed only that test, and reran the full requested check. The rerun passed. The remote check takes several minutes because it builds the RepoOS image environment and runs the scoped suite on ThinkPad; I waited for it to complete rather than treating the queue or running state as a failure.

There is no evidence from a live Android SDK/Gradle host, the Tiao checkout, or a real multi-host queue in this session. The fixture test verifies shell dispatch and artifact output, while the repo's changed-path check verifies the implementation and suite. A human or a follow-up runner task still needs to provide device/toolchain and live pool proof before claiming those environmental scenarios were exercised.

## Key learnings

Docker image ENTRYPOINT semantics are part of the command contract. A `docker run IMAGE command args...` test that only inspects its string can miss a successful no-op when the image already supplies an interpreter entrypoint. Regression tests should observe the actual argv boundary and execute the command path through a controlled shim.

Remote gate results need two independent signals: whether the project gate actually began, and the process exit status. Reserved setup codes can then remain retryable infrastructure outcomes while project commands retain their own exit codes, even when they happen to match those reserved numbers. Finally, runner implementation fields must stay separate from dispatch capabilities so projects route based on actual tools and operating system rather than how a host launches a command.
